column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 25: “The people of wealth have taken the rewards”

column2: From Abū Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him): Some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the Prophet ﷺ:

Messenger of Allah, the people of wealth have taken all the rewards. They pray as we pray, they fast as we fast, and they give charity from their surplus wealth. He said: “Has Allah not given you something to give in charity?

Every tasbīḥah [subḥān Allāh] is a charity, every takbīrah [Allāhu akbar] is a charity, every taḥmīdah [al-ḥamdu lillāh] is a charity and every tahlīlah [lā ilāha illā Allāh] is a charity; enjoining what is right is a charity, forbidding what is wrong is a charity, and in the intimate relations of each of you [with his wife] there is a charity.”
They said: Messenger of Allah, does one of us satisfy his desire and have a reward for it?
He said: “Tell me: if he were to put it in something unlawful, would he not bear a sin for it?
Likewise, when he puts it in what is lawful, he has a reward.” Muslim reported it.

Muslim recorded this hadith through the narration of Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, from Abū al-Aswad al-Dīlī, from Abū Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him). Its meaning has also been narrated from Abū Dharr by many routes, with additions and omissions; we shall mention some of them later, if Allah the Exalted wills.

This hadith shows that the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), because of their intense eagerness for righteous deeds and their strong desire for good, used to grieve over any good they were unable to do that others could do.
So the poor grieved at missing out on giving charity from wealth, which the rich were able to do, and grieved at staying behind when others went out on jihād,

because they lacked the means to equip themselves. Allah has told of this about them in His Book, saying: “Nor [is there blame] on those who, when they came to you to be given mounts and you said, ‘I can find nothing to mount you on,’ turned away with their eyes overflowing with tears, grieving that they could find nothing to spend” [al-Tawbah 9:92].

In this hadith the poor felt a wholesome envy of the people of al-duthūr — al-duthūr meaning wealth — for the reward they gained from giving charity with their wealth, and the Prophet ﷺ directed them to forms of charity within their power.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayrah: The poor among the Emigrants came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: The people of wealth have taken the highest degrees and lasting bliss. He said: “And how is that?”
They said: They pray as we pray and fast as we fast, but they give charity and we do not, and they free slaves and we do not. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
“Shall I not teach you something by which you will catch up with those who have gone ahead of you and get ahead of those after you, and none will be better than you except one who does as you do?”

They said: Certainly, Messenger of Allah. He said: “Say subḥān Allāh, Allāhu akbar and al-ḥamdu lillāh after every prayer, thirty-three times.” Abū Ṣāliḥ said: The poor among the Emigrants came back to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said:
Our brothers, the people of wealth, heard what we were doing and did the same. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills.”
Something like this hadith has been narrated by a number of the Companions, among them ʿAlī, Abū Dharr, Abū al-Dardāʾ, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās and others.
What this means is that the poor thought there was no charity except with wealth, which they were unable to give; so the Prophet ﷺ told them that every kind of good and kindness one does is charity.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Ḥudhayfah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every good deed (maʿrūf) is a charity.”
Al-Bukhārī recorded it from the hadith of Jābir, from the Prophet ﷺ.
So “charity” is applied to every kind of good and kindness one does — so much so that the grace of Allah that reaches His servants is His charity to them.

One of the Salaf used to reject this, saying: Charity comes only from one who seeks its recompense and reward. But the correct view is otherwise. The Prophet ﷺ said concerning shortening the prayer on a journey:

“It is a charity Allah has given you, so accept His charity.” Muslim recorded it. He also said: “Whoever is accustomed to praying at night and is overcome by sleep and sleeps through it, Allah writes for him the reward of his prayer, and his sleep is a charity Allah has given him.”
Al-Nasāʾī and others recorded it from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, and Ibn Mājah recorded it from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ.
In the Musnads of Baqī ibn Makhlad and al-Bazzār, from the hadith of Abū Dharr, as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ):
“There is no day, night or hour but Allah has a charity in it which He bestows on whomever He wills of His servants; and Allah has bestowed nothing on a servant like inspiring him to remember Him.”
Khālid ibn Maʿdān said: Allah gives a charity every day, and Allah has given none of His creation anything in charity better than giving him in charity His remembrance.

Charity without wealth is of two kinds. The first is that which carries kindness over to others, so that it is a charity to them; it may even be better than charity with wealth. Examples are enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, for that is a call to obey Allah

and a restraint from disobeying Him, which is better than benefiting people with wealth. Likewise teaching beneficial knowledge, teaching the Qurʾān, removing harm from the road, striving to bring benefit to people and to ward off harm from them, and likewise supplicating for the Muslims and seeking forgiveness for them.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded, with a chain containing weakness, from Ibn ʿUmar as marfūʿ: “Whoever has wealth, let him give charity from his wealth; whoever has strength, let him give charity from his strength; and whoever has knowledge, let him give charity from his knowledge.” Perhaps it is mawqūf (stopping short of the Prophet ﷺ).
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, with a chain containing weakness, from Samurah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The best charity is the tongue.” He was asked: Messenger of Allah, what is the charity of the tongue?
He said: “Intercession by which you free a captive, spare blood, bring good and kindness to your brother, and ward off something hateful from him.”
ʿAmr ibn Dīnār said: It has reached us that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“There is no charity more beloved to Allah than words. Have you not heard His words, Exalted is He: ‘A kind word and forgiveness are better than a charity followed by injury’ [al-Baqarah 2:263]?” Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded it.
Among the mursal reports of al-Ḥasan, the Prophet ﷺ said: “It is part of charity that you greet people with a cheerful face.”
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it.
Muʿādh said: Teaching knowledge to one who does not know it is a charity. It has also been narrated as marfūʿ.
Among the kinds of charity is refraining from harming people. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Dharr: I said: Messenger of Allah, which deeds are best?
He said: “Faith, and jihād in His path.” I said: Which slaves are best to free?
He said: “The most precious to their owners and the highest in price.” I said: And if I cannot do that?
He said: “Help a craftsman, or make something for one who is unskilled.”
I said: Messenger of Allah, what if I am too weak for some of these deeds?
He said: “Keep your evil from people, for that is a charity.”

Further additions have been narrated in the hadith of Abū Dharr. Al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Dharr, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Your smiling in your brother's face is a charity for you;

your enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is a charity; your guiding a man in a land where people lose their way is a charity for you; your removing stones, thorns and bones from the road is a charity for you; and your pouring from your bucket into your brother's bucket is a charity for you.”
Ibn Ḥibbān recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of Abū Dharr, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “There is no soul of the son of Ādam but owes a charity every day on which the sun rises.”
He was asked: Messenger of Allah, where are we to find a charity to give?
He said: “The doors of good are many: tasbīḥ, takbīr, taḥmīd and tahlīl; enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong; removing harm from the road; making the deaf hear; guiding the blind;

directing one who seeks his need to it; hurrying on your two legs with one in distress who is calling for help; and carrying with the strength of your two arms along with the weak. All of this is charity from you to yourself.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Abū Dharr, who said: I said: Messenger of Allah, the rich have taken the reward; they give charity and we do not. He said: “And in you there is charity: your lifting a bone from the road is a charity,

your guiding someone on the road is a charity, your helping the weak with your surplus strength is a charity, your speaking for one who cannot express himself is a charity, and your intercourse with your wife is a charity.” I said: Messenger of Allah, we satisfy our desire and are rewarded?! He said:
“Tell me: if he put it in something unlawful, would he not be sinning?”
He said: I said: Yes. He said: “Do you then count the evil and not count the good?”
In another narration the Prophet ﷺ said: “There is much charity in you” — and he mentioned the surplus of your hearing and the surplus of your sight. In another narration of Imam Aḥmad's he said:

“Among the doors of charity are takbīr, subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh and astaghfiru Allāh; enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong; moving thorns, bones and stones out of people's way;

guiding the blind; making the deaf and the dumb hear until he understands; directing one who seeks a need to it when you know where it is; hurrying on your two legs to one in distress who is calling for help;

and lifting with the strength of your two arms along with the weak. All of these are doors of charity from you to yourself. And in your intercourse with your wife there is a reward for you.” I said: How can there be a reward for me in my desire?
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Tell me: if you had a child who reached maturity, and you hoped for good from him, and then he died, would you hope for reward from Allah for him?
I said: Yes. He said: Did you create him?
I said: No, Allah created him. He said: Did you guide him?
I said: No, Allah guided him. He said: Did you provide for him?

I said: No, Allah provided for him. He said: Likewise, then: put it in what is lawful and keep it from what is unlawful; if Allah wills, He will give it life, and if He wills, He will cause it to die, and you will have a reward.”
The apparent sense of this version entails that he is rewarded for intercourse with his wife when he intends to seek a child, for whose upbringing and education during his life reward follows,
and whom he counts with Allah at his death. But when he intends nothing in satisfying his desire, people have disputed whether that is included in this hadith.
It is authentically reported that a man's spending on his family is a charity. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Masʿūd al-Anṣārī, the Prophet ﷺ said: “A man's spending on his family is a charity.”

In a narration of Muslim's: “while he seeks reward for it”; and in a wording of al-Bukhārī's: “When a man spends on his family seeking reward for it, it is a charity for him.” This shows that he is rewarded for it only when he seeks its reward from Allah, as in the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ,
that the Prophet ﷺ said: “You will never spend anything seeking by it the Face of Allah but you will be rewarded for it — even the morsel you raise to your wife's mouth.” Both recorded it.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Thawbān, the Prophet ﷺ said:

“The best of dīnārs is a dīnār a man spends on his dependants, a dīnār he spends on a horse in the path of Allah, and a dīnār a man spends on his companions in the path of Allah.” When narrating this hadith Abū Qilābah said:
He began with dependants. And what man has a greater reward than a man who spends on young dependants of his, through whom Allah keeps them from need and makes them self-sufficient?
It also has, from Saʿd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Your spending on your dependants is a charity, and what your wife eats from your wealth is a charity.”
In the other narration this is qualified by seeking the Face of Allah.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “A dīnār you spend in the path of Allah,
a dīnār you spend on freeing a slave, a dīnār you give in charity to a poor person, and a dīnār you spend on your family: the best of them is the dīnār you spend on your family.”

Imam Aḥmad, and Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ, recorded from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Give charity.” A man said: I have a dīnār. He said: “Give it in charity to yourself.” He said:

I have another dīnār. He said: “Give it in charity to your wife.” He said: I have another dīnār. He said: “Give it in charity to your child.” He said: I have another dīnār. He said: “Give it in charity to your servant.” He said: I have another dīnār. He said: “You know best.”
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whatever you feed yourself is a charity for you; whatever you feed your child

is a charity for you; whatever you feed your wife is a charity for you; and whatever you feed your servant is a charity for you.” There are many hadiths with this meaning; it would take too long to mention them.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: “No Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop from which a person, a bird or an animal eats but it is a charity for him.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Jābir, the Prophet ﷺ said: “No Muslim plants a tree but whatever is eaten from it is a charity for him,

whatever is stolen from it is a charity for him, whatever a wild beast eats from it is a charity for him, whatever the birds eat is a charity for him, and no one takes anything from it but it is a charity for him.”
In another narration of his: “…and no person, animal or bird eats from it but it is a charity for him until the Day of Resurrection.”
In the Musnad, with a weak chain, from Muʿādh ibn Anas al-Juhanī, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever builds a building without injustice or transgression,
or plants a planting without injustice or transgression, will have a continuing reward so long as any of the creatures of the Most Merciful benefits from it.”

Al-Bukhārī mentioned in his Tārīkh, from the hadith of Jābir as marfūʿ: “Whoever digs for water, no thirsty liver — of jinn, human, wild beast or bird — drinks from it but Allah will reward him on the Day of Resurrection.”

The apparent sense of all these hadiths indicates that these things are a charity for which the sower, the planter and the like are rewarded without any purpose or intention. Likewise the words of the Prophet ﷺ, “Tell me: if he put it in what is unlawful, would he not bear a sin for it?

Likewise, when he puts it in what is lawful, he has a reward,” indicate by their apparent sense that he is rewarded for going to his wife without any intention; for the one who has intercourse with his wife is like the sower who ploughs the earth and sows seed in it.

A group of scholars held this view, and Abū Muḥammad ibn Qutaybah inclined to it with regard to eating, drinking and intercourse, citing as evidence the Prophet's words ﷺ: “The believer is rewarded in everything, even in the morsel he raises to his mouth.”

But this wording that he cited as evidence is not known; what is known is the Prophet's saying ﷺ to Saʿd, “You will never spend anything seeking by it the Face of Allah but you will be rewarded for it,
even the morsel you raise to your wife's mouth,” which is qualified by sincere intention for Allah; so the unqualified hadiths are to be understood in its light. And Allah knows best.

This is also shown by the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: “There is no good in much of their private conversation, except for one who enjoins charity, or what is right, or setting things right between people; and whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah — We shall give him a great reward” [al-Nisāʾ 4:114].
He called that good, but made the reward follow from it only with a sincere intention.
As for doing it to show off, one is punished for it. The point at issue is only when one does it with no intention, either good or bad.

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: Whoever does a good deed without an intention, his intention in choosing Islam over other religions suffices him. The apparent sense of this is that he is rewarded for it without any intention at all,
because by entering Islam he has chosen deeds of good in general, so he is rewarded for every such deed he does by virtue of that intention. And Allah knows best.
His words: “Tell me: if he put it in what is unlawful, would he not bear a sin for it?
Likewise, when he puts it in what is lawful, he has a reward.”

This is what the scholars of legal theory call reverse analogy (qiyās al-ʿaks). Of this kind is Ibn Masʿūd's saying: The Prophet ﷺ said one thing and I said another. He said, “Whoever dies associating anything with Allah will enter the Fire,” and I said: Whoever dies not associating anything with Allah will enter Paradise.
The second kind of non-monetary charity is that whose benefit is confined to the one who does it, such as the various forms of remembrance: takbīr, tasbīḥ, taḥmīd, tahlīl and seeking forgiveness.
Walking to the mosques is likewise a charity. None of the hadiths mentions prayer, fasting, Ḥajj or jihād as being a charity, though most of these deeds are better than charities of wealth;

for he mentioned these only in answer to the question of the poor, who asked him what could match the voluntary giving of the rich from their wealth; as for the obligatory duties, they all shared in them.
The texts are abundant in preferring remembrance to charity with wealth and to other deeds, as in the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Shall I not tell you of the best of your deeds, the purest of them in the sight of your King, the highest of them in raising your degrees, better for you than spending gold and silver, and better for you than meeting your enemy and striking their necks while they strike yours?”
They said: Certainly, Messenger of Allah. He said: “The remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.”
Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded it, and Mālik mentioned it in the Muwaṭṭaʾ as mawqūf, the words of Abū al-Dardāʾ.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Whoever says, ‘There is no god but Allah alone, without partner; His is the dominion and His is the praise; He gives life and causes death, and He has power over all things,’ a hundred times in a day, it will be for him equal to freeing ten slaves;

a hundred good deeds will be written for him and a hundred bad deeds erased from him; and it will be a protection for him from Satan that day until evening. No one will bring anything better than what he brought, except someone who has done more than that.”
Both also have, from Abū Ayyūb, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever says it ten times is like one who has freed four souls of the descendants of Ismāʿīl.”
Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd, that the Prophet ﷺ was asked: Which of the servants will be highest in rank with Allah on the Day of Resurrection?
He said: “Those who remember Allah much.” I said: Messenger of Allah, even above the one who fights in the path of Allah?
He said: “Even if he struck the disbelievers and idolaters with his sword until it broke and he was dyed with blood, those who remember Allah would be higher than him in rank.”
Something similar is narrated from the hadiths of Muʿādh and Jābir as marfūʿ, but the correct view is that it is mawqūf, Muʿādh's own words.

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of Abū al-Wāziʿ, from Abū Burdah, from Abū Mūsā, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “If a man had dirhams in his lap that he was distributing, and another was remembering Allah, the one remembering Allah would be better.”
I say: The correct version is from Abū al-Wāziʿ, from Abū Barzah al-Aslamī, as his own words.
Jaʿfar al-Firyābī recorded it.

He also recorded, from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever says Allāhu akbar a hundred times, subḥān Allāh a hundred times and lā ilāha illā Allāh a hundred times, it will be better for him than ten slaves he frees and seven sacrificial camels he slaughters.”
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded with his chain that Abū al-Dardāʾ was told: A man has freed a hundred slaves. He said: A hundred slaves from one man's wealth is a great deal;
but better than that is faith held to night and day, and that the tongue of each of you remain moist with the remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Abū al-Dardāʾ also said: To say Allāhu akbar a hundred times is dearer to me than to give a hundred dīnārs in charity.
Salmān al-Fārisī and others of the Companions and Successors likewise said that remembrance is better than giving the same number [of coins] in charity.
Imam Aḥmad and al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of Umm Hāniʾ, that the Prophet ﷺ said to her:

“Glorify Allah a hundred times, for that equals a hundred slaves of the descendants of Ismāʿīl. Praise Allah a hundred times, for that equals for you a hundred bridled and saddled horses on which you mount [fighters] in the path of Allah. Magnify Allah a hundred times, for that equals for you a hundred sacrificial camels, garlanded and accepted.

And declare Allah's oneness a hundred times” — I can only think that he said — “it fills what is between heaven and earth; and no one's deed will be raised that day like yours, unless he brings the like of what you brought.”
Aḥmad also recorded it, as did Ibn Mājah, and in their version: “And say lā ilāha illā Allāh a hundred times; it leaves no sin, and no deed surpasses it.”
Al-Tirmidhī recorded something similar from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ.
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās as marfūʿ: “No charity is better than the remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.”

Al-Firyābī recorded, with a chain open to question, from Abū Umāmah as marfūʿ: “Whoever misses out on toiling through the night [in prayer], is too miserly with his wealth to spend it, or too cowardly to fight the enemy,

let him say subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdihi often, for it is more beloved to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, than a mountain of gold or a mountain of silver spent in the path of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.”

Al-Bazzār recorded it with a passable chain, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās as marfūʿ, saying in his narration, “let him remember Allah often,” and adding nothing to that. There are several other hadiths with this meaning.
